extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/aesthetics; scholars studying Kantian theories of taste, art, and genius
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria from Kant's Critique of Judgment for judging beauty, distinguishing types of art, and defining genius and taste; useful for evaluating or producing aesthetic objects according to Kantian standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal communicability of a pleasure carries with it that the pleasure is not one of enjoyment from mere sensation but must be derived from reflection; aesthetical art has for standard the reflective Judgement and not sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic pleasure that counts as beautiful should be communicable universally — not contingent on individual sensation. Examples: reflective satisfaction in judging form rather than sensual enjoyment. Anti-pattern: pleasures grounded only in sensory enjoyment (mere charm, table entertainments) are 'pleasant' not 'beautiful'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of taste judge forms without the aid of concepts and find satisfaction in the mere act of judgement; such judgements are made without being based on or producing any interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true judgement of taste must be free from personal, empirical, or utilitarian interest (no desire for possession, social advantage, or empirical benefit). Anti-patterns: vanity, social prestige, or direct utility informing the judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate vs mediate interest in beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: An immediate interest in the Beautiful is one that arises without reference to further ends (especially as in Nature); a mediate interest is bound up with reference to society or other inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty can arouse immediate interest (pleasing in itself). Artificial beauty or objects regarded as means to social ends arouse mediate interest (e.g., adornment for vanity). Example/anti-pattern: if a person is deceived into thinking an artificial object is natural, once deception is discovered the immediate interest disappears and may be replaced by vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic vs moral feeling distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in the mere aesthetical judgement is called that of taste, whereas the pleasure arising from judgements of practical maxims is moral feeling; the two are specifically different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic satisfaction is independent of concepts and interest; moral judgement derives from concepts and produces an interest tied to reason. Recognize the different grounds and avoid conflating taste with moral goodness without further argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in natural beauty as indicator of moral disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: To take an immediate interest in the beauty of Nature (not merely to have taste in judging it) is always a mark of a good soul and indicates a frame of mind favorable to moral feeling when voluntarily bound up with contemplation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitual, immediate appreciation of natural beauty suggests a disposition open to moral cultivation. Caveat: interest in beautifying art or charms used for vanity does not have this moral indication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that natural beauty be perceived as natural
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate interest in natural beauty is based on the thought that nature has produced it; if the object is known to be artificial, the immediate interest vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating natural beauty, consider whether perceivers regard it as produced by nature. Example: planting artificial flowers or placing carved birds deceives and upon discovery removes immediate interest; anti-pattern: appreciating an object only because of its artificial provenance or social display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art must seem like nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In a product of beautiful art we must be conscious that it is Art and not Nature; yet the purposiveness in its form must seem as free from rule as if it were a product of mere nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should give the impression of purposiveness without appearing contrived by explicit rules. Anti-patterns: art where school-formulae or technical rules painfully obtrude; explicit visible fettering of mental powers by rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (aesthetical purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art is purposive for itself, and although devoid of definite purpose, it furthers the culture of the mental powers in reference to social communication — purposiveness without purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish works aimed merely at sensation or at a definite utilitarian object (mechanical or pleasant art) from those where form purposively serves no concrete external purpose. Evaluate whether the object's purposiveness appears self-contained and reflective rather than instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art must not seem designed
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposiveness in the product of beautiful art, although designed, must not seem designed; beautiful art must look like nature, although we are conscious of it as art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic form should not reveal the rule or design that produced it; it must appear free and spontaneous. Anti-pattern: forms where the rule is 'punctiliously observed' and painfully apparent (schoolishness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as innate rule-giver
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the innate mental disposition (ingenium) through which Nature gives the rule to Art; it is the talent which gives the rule to Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius is understood as an inborn productive faculty that supplies original rules to art rather than following precepts. For producers: value originality and rule-giving capacity over mere skill-instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as the primary property of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is a talent for producing that for which no definite rule can be given; originality must be its first property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine genius produces original forms not derivable from explicit rules. Anti-pattern: mistaking high teachable skill or learned imitation for genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary (model) character of genius' products
rubrics_metrics.description: Because genius can produce original nonsense as well as original excellence, its products must be models (exemplary) and ought not to spring from imitation but must serve as a standard or rule of judgement for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works of genius serve as paradigms to be imitated in spirit rather than copied in detail. Evaluate whether a work can be abstracted into a model that evokes similar faculties in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability of genius to communicate methodically
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius cannot describe or indicate scientifically how it brings about its products; the author does not know how he has come by his Ideas and cannot produce them at will or teach others by precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A creative process that resists codification is characteristic of genius. Anti-pattern: claims that brilliant aesthetic production can be fully taught by stepwise precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a mechanical element (technique) in art
rubrics_metrics.description: In all free arts there is yet requisite something compulsory, or 'mechanism', without which the spirit would have no body: e.g., in poetry there must be accuracy of language, prosody and metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even genius-based beautiful art requires learned technique and rules for execution. Anti-pattern: the belief that removing all constraints produces the best art; practice must include cultivated skill and schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between art, handicraft, and science
rubrics_metrics.description: Art (facere) is production through freedom grounded in reason; science (can from know) is theoretical; handicraft is mercenary and often compulsory — art differs from mere technical know-how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by whether they originate from free purposive reason (art) versus learned, rule-bound production (handicraft) or theoretical knowledge (science). Example: a product of bees may be analogized to art but is nature/instinct, not human art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant art vs beautiful art
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant arts are directed merely to enjoyment (sensation) e.g., entertaining storytelling, table arrangement, music as pleasant noise; beautiful art is a mode of representation purposive for itself and furthers culture of mental powers for social communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transient entertainment from art aimed at reflective judgement and communicable pleasure. Anti-pattern: confusing social convivial amusements with beautiful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is the faculty of judging, not producing
rubrics_metrics.description: For judging beautiful objects as such, taste is requisite; for production of such objects, genius is requisite. Taste is a judging faculty that can be cultivated and used to check and improve art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should cultivate taste to refine execution; judges should recognize taste as a cultivated capacity, not a set of production rules. Example: an artist uses taste (trained by examples) to arrive at satisfying form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Ideas and 'spirit' animate art
rubrics_metrics.description: Spirit in an aesthetical sense is the animating principle of the mind; aesthetical Ideas are representations of the Imagination that occasion much thought without being capturable by definite concepts and thus animate works with 'spirit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's power to evoke rich, inexhaustible imaginative thought (aesthetic Ideas) indicates 'spirit' and distinguishes spirited art from merely neat, elegant but lifeless products. For evaluators: assess the capacity of a work to provoke thought beyond conceptual containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on representing ugliness (disgust exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial beauty can represent many things, even things in nature that are ugly or calamitous, but one kind of ugliness cannot be represented without destroying aesthetic satisfaction: that which excites disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art can aestheticize the Furies, disease, war, etc., but representations that provoke disgust break the aesthetic distance and cannot be regarded as beautiful. Example: sculpture avoids direct representation of disgusting forms and uses allegory or pleasing attributes instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art can render disagreeable subjects aesthetically pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art shows its superiority in that it can describe as beautiful things which may in nature be ugly or displeasing (e.g., the Furies, war), by representation and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the artist's form and representation transform a disagreeable subject into an aesthetic object without provoking disgust; evaluate use of allegory, form, and stylization in masking literal repulsiveness.
